podcast.body: An alternate version of this song was widely available through file-sharing in the early 2000s, enabling fans to obtain it for free online before it became officially available. "YouTube with an alternate version of I Will Follow that was there for the taking through file sharing back in the early 2000s."

podcast.body: The song emerged from a particularly "loud and violent argument" Bono had with The Edge during rehearsals. Bono reportedly felt The Edge was playing his guitar parts "too gentle," so he snatched the guitar and demonstrated how it should be played, leading to the song's distinctive sound. "The song itself came out of a very loud and very violent argument that Bono had with the edge during rehearsals."

podcast.body: The song's emotional core is rooted in the unconditional love a mother has for a son, but it also delves into the pain of a son being separated or "taken away" from his mother. Bono was actually singing the song from his mother's point of view, and the lyrics can be interpreted as resembling a suicide note, a possibility Bono himself acknowledges. "Bono was actually singing the song from his mother's point of view."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The song's genesis dates back to September 10th, 1974, when Bono's mother, Iris Hussin, passed away from a cerebral hemorrhage, only days after her father (Bono's grandfather, Alex) also died. This double tragedy profoundly affected a 13-year-old Bono, leading him into a period of anger, confusion, and isolation, which became the emotional wellspring for the lyrics. "This is where I will follow comes from."

podcast.body: This, U2's first big single from the *Boy* album, is noted for having had "a difficult birth," requiring "a long, long time to get right." An early, previously lost recording of the song from 1980, where the band "hadn't quite got things to where they needed them to be," was officially released on the 2008 Deluxe reissue of the *Boy* album. "Here's a recording of the song where they hadn't quite got things to where they needed them to be."
